Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to fresh inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

Sources indicate that on Friday, the Bureau of Labor Statistics released the Producer Price Index for October, which tracks the change in prices that U.S. producers are able to get for their products. This is one way to measure inflation on the market end, rather than the consumer end.

The results were mixed. While prices didn’t rise quite as high as economists anticipated month-over-month (0.3% vs. 0.4%), year-over-year price growth did reach 6.5% — the largest increase in four years. This points to even higher costs for consumers coming in the near future.

Investors are convinced that the Federal Reserve will raise overnight borrowing rates again in December to pull inflation down. And higher overnight borrowing rates — called the federal funds rate, which is what banks pay to fund products like mortgages — usually lead to higher mortgage rates.

The Flipper One is more than a Zero 2.0 – it’s a $399 Linux computer with a $13M Kickstarter

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the Flipper One crowdfunding campaign has broken the $13-million mark, smashing the funding raised for previous Flipper devices and demonstrating strong interest in the successor to the Flipper Zero.
  • The thing that made the Flipper Zero so popular was how easy it was to use.
  • Also: The Flipper One may be the ultimate Linux PC for hackers in 2026 – and I’m excited.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the Flipper One crowdfunding campaign has broken the $13-million mark, smashing the funding raised for previous Flipper devices and demonstrating strong interest in the successor to the Flipper Zero. The $399 Flipper One is a pocket Linux computer focused on networking, with delivery estimated for July 2027. But it isn’t simply an updated version of the Flipper Zero. It’s a very different animal and a much more serious bit of kit.

The thing that made the Flipper Zero so popular was how easy it was to use. You could fire it up and turn the volume down on the TV at your parents’ place, see the radio waves coming from your car’s key fob, and copy hotel room key cards.

Also: The Flipper One may be the ultimate Linux PC for hackers in 2026 – and I’m excited.

Industry observers note that it could do a lot, there wasn’t a steep learning curve, and you didn’t need to buy anything else. Did the fake videos on TikTok from people claiming they could change the prices at gas stations (I wish!) or start cars remotely help make the Zero more popular?

Unfortunately, yes. But what made it successful was that it packed a lot of power into a package that was small, fun, affordable, and easy to use.

If the Flipper Zero, with its NFC, RFID, sub-GHz, and IR, was kindergarten, the Flipper One is a college degree: a pocket Linux computer focused on networking.

This is reflected in the price. You can pick up a Zero for $169, while the Flipper One is $399.

What this buys you is the Flipper One base computer with a 256 × 144 grayscale LCD, Rockchip RK3576 8-core ARM SoC with NPU, a low-power MCU for handling the LCD and user interface, 8GB of LPDDR5 RAM, 64GB of UFS 2.2 storage, and a microSD slot.

If that $399 feels like a lot, it’s worth keeping in mind that, according to Flipper, the price only covers production costs and that the RAM and UFS storage account for at least half of the total hardware cost.

Recent findings suggest that if you think this is a lot, you could spend a lot more. Adding a LoRa, SDR, or 5G module will push the total up a lot higher. And if you want all three modules, you’re looking at $759 for the Flipper One Ultimate Bundle.

Also: The Flipper One is the Linux cyberdeck I wish my Raspberry Pi could be.

Industry observers note that the reception has been strong enough that pledges have flown past the $300,000 goal that Flipper initially set, with over 24,000 backers pledging over $13 million. Close to 5,300 backers have gone for the Ultimate Bundle, compared to just over 4,300 choosing the bare Flipper One.

This suggests that backers really want the radio capabilities that this latest platform offers.

If you want one, this crowdfunding run is a good time to get one because it’s a Kickstarter Special slashing 25% off an estimated retail price of $550.

The response over on Reddit has been a little more subdued, with some being taken aback by the price of the Zero’s bigger sibling.

Also: 7 useful things I can do with my Flipper Zero – as someone who’s used it for years.

As someone who homebrews a lot of electronics, I’m going to say that the price is justified, and this project goes far beyond something you could put together with a Raspberry Pi and some code.

Sources indicate that the Flipper One campaign runs until Dec. 17, 2026, with delivery estimated for July 2027.

In a recent development, keep in mind that this is a Kickstarter pledge, not a purchase, and that rewards aren’t guaranteed. Flipper also says on the Kickstarter page that component shortages are the biggest risk to the project and that they “could cause significant delays to production and delivery.” It also says that if RAM prices continue to rise, it cannot “rule out adjusting some product specifications, including reducing the amount of RAM.”.

Also: Is the Flipper Zero the best multi-tool for hacking?

And the good news here is that I’ve seen several analysts predicting that RAM prices will begin to go down in 2027 as demand eases off.

Tech Report: Black Friday Sales Are Days Away, but Most US Adults Aren’t Waiting, CNET Finds

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1460 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cnet

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that even though early holiday sales started months ago, shopping your wish lists during Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales may be worth the wait if you’re one of the few planning to shop November sales.
  • CNET’s annual holiday shopping survey indicates that 27% of US adults plan to start holiday shopping in November and 17% plan to shop during sales.
  • Finding savings is paramount to staying within your price range this year, but how can you spot a good deal when nearly every retailer is having a sale?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that even though early holiday sales started months ago, shopping your wish lists during Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales may be worth the wait if you’re one of the few planning to shop November sales. It’s the time to save money on most tech devices. But holiday shopping could look different for US adults juggling smaller budgets and shopping frustrations.

CNET’s annual holiday shopping survey indicates that 27% of US adults plan to start holiday shopping in November and 17% plan to shop during sales. However, US adults will be juggling a smaller tech budget of $808. That’s $123 less than CNET’s survey findings last year.

Finding savings is paramount to staying within your price range this year, but how can you spot a good deal when nearly every retailer is having a sale? CNET experts weighed in on US adults’ holiday shopping plans and shared expert advice to score the best Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals on must-haves.

CNET found that 27% will initiative or start their holiday shopping this month, with 17% of November shoppers planning to shop holiday sales, like Black Friday and Cyber Monday.

Industry observers note that the massive question is whether the sales are worthwhile. CNET’s director of commerce content, Russell Holly, notes it comes down to when you find a deal on a must-have item.

“The best time to buy is the moment you see something you want on an actual discount, because increased prices can come at any time,” Holly said.

Holly says even steep discounts aren’t lowering prices as much as before, but the right deals may make you reconsider. You just have to know where and when to shop for tech devices.

For example, Black Friday is usually the best time to buy electronics, including TVs and robot vacuums, with the biggest deals lasting from Black Friday to Cyber Monday.

CNET’s senior laptops editor, Matt Elliott, notes if you’re planning to buy a fresh laptop during holiday sales, look for discounts at Amazon, Best Buy and vendor sites like Dell, HP and Lenovo.

“These retailers and companies are constantly rotating discounts on laptops, and these sales can save you hundreds of dollars. So, it’s worth tracking the price of a laptop you want and buying it when it dips,” noted Elliott.

Black Friday and Cyber Monday are also a good time to buy the latest wearables, remarked CNET’s wearable expert, Vanessa Hand Orellana.

“For Black Friday, all the heavy wearable hitters tend to go on sale: Google, Samsung, Oura, Garmin and Apple,” stated Orellana. However, if you don’t need the latest tech, you can find some of the best deals on last year’s tech at third-party retailers, like Best Buy and Walmart. And many of the previous-gen models share the same features as the newest ones, said Orellana.

CNET’s deals team spends hours making sure sales are legitimate — not just a fake price drop. And in the coming weeks, they’ll track deals on devices like laptops, headphones, wearable devices and smart home gadgets, plus alternatives to more costly tech, to help you determine what’s worth buying now or later.

You can also check an item’s price history to see if you’re getting the best deal by using price trackers like CamelCamelCamel and comparing prices across retailers before buying. But as Holly noted, if you want to upgrade your personal devices, don’t wait. Look for the best price you can find and buy it right away. Otherwise, prices may go up while you wait.

Industry observers note that last year, CNET found that US adults planned to spend an average of $931 on holiday shopping. This year, shoppers are planning to spend less.

Industry observers note that on average, they expect to spend $808 on holiday shopping. That’s $123 less than last year. Some generations proposal to spend more, such as millennials, who anticipate an average holiday shopping outlay of $1,074. Boomers will spend around half that amount — $582.

Higher everyday living costs could explain why holiday budgets are lower.“Everything else being more expensive means less left over for gifts,” said Holly. “There’s very little indication that component prices are going to come back down anytime soon, so if you’re hoping for the kinds of prices you saw even two years ago, I would say you’re going to be waiting quite a while.”.

It has been revealed that balancing holiday gifts and everyday basics on your usual income can be a lot to handle. Now’s the time to set holiday expectations, including a budget and a list of must-haves, along with more affordable options that still meet your needs.

Sources indicate that then keep checking prices and deals from your trusted retailers and be prepared to buy when you spot good savings. Most importantly, try to avoid using credit cards and buy-now, pay-later looks that can lead to debt. The Federal Reserve’s recent rate hike held rates elevated, which means borrowing costs will remain high and make debt more expensive through higher credit card and loan interest rates.

CNET found that 73% of shoppers plan to buy tech products or services this season, but what most US adults plan to buy and how much they plan to spend may surprise you.

In a recent development, thirty percent of shoppers initiative to purchase toys, and 25% plan to buy kitchen items, such as air fryers and cookware. But shoppers don’t plan to buy as many personal electronics and home entertainment products. Only 20% plan to buy headphones or earbuds, and even fewer plan to buy video games for consoles (18%) or laptops and TVs (11%). More shocking is that only 13% plan to buy phones. We’ve seen prices increase across popular tech devices and brands due to the RAM shortage, which has led to low supply and high demand for memory chips.

Recent findings suggest that some of the latest releases cost way more than the average $808 most US adults plan to spend. For instance, the $2,000 iPhone Duo alone costs even more than the average $1,704 that millennials plan to spend on tech this holiday season. And less costly phones are still beyond holiday budgets, like the $1,200 iPhone 18 Pro Max, and even the iPhone 18 Pro is $1,200. Trade-in offers and sales can help lower that cost if you’re planning to upgrade, but shop around and compare deals before buying.

Increased prices may make you reconsider whether to stick with your current model or upgrade, but remember, you have options.

“If the current laptop works well enough, upgrading can either be viewed as a luxury purchase for later or shifted to buying used or refurbished models to save extra,” Holly said.

You may also consider a slightly older model of the device you’re looking for. It could still have all of the features you need, but cost less. Another money-saving option is to consider refurbished tech that’s in excellent or good condition from a certified refurbished retailer. You may still notice some price increases due to demand, but it could still cost less than the newest models.

According to recent reports, most US shoppers (84%) expect the holiday shopping season to come with a few hurdles this year. Forty-three percent are concerned about deceptive pricing practices, such as retailers raising original prices before discounting them for a sale. Others are concerned about deals selling out immediately because of low stock or automated buying bots (39%).

But if you’re more worried about fake deals or sales being a money grab by retailers, Holly said that historically, there have been some great sales ahead of the holidays. It’s still best to do your research before buying to make sure you’re getting a deal by comparing retailer prices before and after declared sales and using price tracking tools, like CamelCamelCamel. Heads up that many retailers, like Amazon, have flash sales with specific times of deeper discounts, and you’ll need to act fast, so it’s best to initiative your holiday shopping now.

“The best thing anyone can do ahead of a shopping event is prepare,” mentioned Holly. “Find your favorite price tracker tool before the event starts, have a general idea of what you’re looking to buy and be sure to keep an eye out for bigger discounts when you bundle things together.”.

CNET commissioned YouGov Plc to conduct the survey. All figures, unless otherwise stated, are from YouGov Plc. The total sample size was 2,615 adults, of whom 1,552 were interested in purchasing consumer tech products or services this winter holiday season. Fieldwork was undertaken Sept. 3-6, 2026. The survey was carried out online. The figures have been weighted and are representative of all US adults (aged 18 and older).

10 stocks we like better than Space Exploration Technologies ›.

CNBC stock analyst and TV personality Jim Cramer is cautious about investing in Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX +1.60%), while Ark Invest CEO and investing head Cathie Wood said in July, "We think this could become the most vital firm in history, and I mean in global history.".

Each of these stock prognosticators has their own following and detractors. Which camp do you fall into?

Deciding whether to invest in SpaceX comes down to what makes sense for an individual investor's situation.

Cramer has told his audience that he has not bought shares for his charitable trust. He's been complimentary toward SpaceX, but he also raised a range of issues in one of his recent Mad Money reveals. He has highlighted SpaceX’s spending costs as well as the complications surrounding a potential merger between SpaceX and Tesla (TSLA +1.50%).

The investment actions differ, but that speaks to each having their own goals, which is the bigger takeaway from this little thought exercise than who is "right.".

NASDAQ · As of 9:41 AM ET 11/19/26.

Retirees, for example, may be more concerned with stability in their investments than with high-risk, high-reward results that could take multiple years (or decades) to pay off, if they do at all. They may then lean more toward Cramer's actions of sitting on the sidelines.

Sources indicate that in the third quarter of 2026, SpaceX's capital expenditures climbed 186% from the prior year to $19.5 billion, with spending only likely to keep climbing. It's also not a profitable organization, reporting a net loss of $413 million for the first nine months of the year. In a retiree's situation, it may make more sense to own shares of a company like JPMorgan Chase (JPM +0.66%), which is profitable and can use earnings for dividend payments and stock buybacks.

A younger investor with a longer time horizon may find the risk-to-reward framework worthwhile and lean toward mimicking Wood's moves. In Q3, SpaceX's revenue grew 161%; sales from what it calls its Super Intelligence segment increased from $813 million to $7.5 billion; and it has financial flexibility, with approximately $90 billion in cash, cash equivalents, and marketable securities.

Recent findings suggest that all the numbers suggest that SpaceX is likely a better fit for investors seeking aggressive growth than for those looking for predictable returns. Keep that in mind as you do further research on this stock.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Erin Kennedy – Updated Nov 19, 2026 at 6:17AM EST.
  • Choosing between established software giants and high-growth security specialists requires a look at different business models.
  • Recent findings suggest that intuit is a financial technology powerhouse serving millions of consumers and small businesses with its tax and accounting platforms.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Erin Kennedy – Updated Nov 19, 2026 at 6:17AM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Intuit ›.

Choosing between established software giants and high-growth security specialists requires a look at different business models. Intuit (INTU +0.55%) and Zscaler (ZS +8.92%) both offer essential tools but serve very different markets.

Recent findings suggest that intuit is a financial technology powerhouse serving millions of consumers and small businesses with its tax and accounting platforms. Zscaler focuses on securing cloud-based networks for large enterprises and government agencies. Comparing them helps you decide between a mature, highly profitable business and a faster-growing cybersecurity innovator.

Intuit is a global leader among tech stocks that provides financial services for consumers and businesses. According to its latest annual report, filed for the fiscal year ended July 31, 2026, the company serves roughly 93 million customers worldwide. Its strategy involves expanding into the mid-market segment and enhancing its platform with AI tools, such as the October 2026 acquisition of Sequence.

Recent findings suggest that intuit's financial performance remains strong across its major segments. In fiscal 2026, revenue reached nearly $21.4 billion, representing growth of approximately 13.9% over the previous year. Intuit reported net income of close to $4.6 billion, resulting in a healthy net margin of roughly 21.3%.

Sources indicate that as of its July 2026 balance sheet, Intuit had a debt-to-equity ratio (total debt divided by equity) of approximately 0.4 and a current ratio of 1.5. Free cash flow, which equals cash flow from operations minus capital expenditures, reached nearly $8.6 billion. Note that stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 23.3% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation, since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

Recent findings suggest that zscaler provides a cloud-native security platform known as the Zero Trust Exchange, which protects consumers and data regardless of location. The cybersecurity specialist serves roughly 11,000 customers globally, including more than half of the Fortune 500 companies. It also pursues technical alliances, such as its recent security collaborations with Nvidia (NVDA +3.88%).

High demand for cybersecurity tools has driven significant top-line growth. In fiscal 2026, revenue reached nearly $3.4 billion, an increase of approximately 25.4% year over year. However, the manufacturer reported a net loss of roughly $63.2 million, resulting in a negative net margin of nearly 1.9%.

As of its July 2026 balance sheet, Zscaler had a debt-to-equity ratio of approximately 0.7 and a current ratio of roughly 1.7. Free cash flow was approximately $852.4 million. Note that stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 72.8% of operating cash flow.

It has been revealed that intuit faces several challenges, including intense competition from both government-provided tax tools and private software rivals. The company relies heavily on the seasonal tax preparation industry, which creates significant revenue concentration in certain months. Cybersecurity threats remain a constant concern, particularly with FTC oversight and potential legal liabilities from ongoing class action litigation.

Zscaler competes in a crowded market against established networking and security vendors like Microsoft (MSFT +2.37%). The organization depends heavily on a network of channel partners to generate a significant portion of its revenue. Managing a global infrastructure of over 200 data centers entails complex operational risks, international regulatory requirements, and potential class action litigation regarding consumer protection claims.

Intuit appears more conservatively valued when looking at its forward P/E, while Zscaler carries a higher P/S ratio that reflects rapid sales growth.

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

My reflex is to find Zscaler more attractive because Intuit seems like part of the old guard of software. Also, Intuit's business model is basically predicated on making it hard for people to file taxes (so they'll pay for Intuit's software), and that's kind of messed up! It's not the equivalent of investing in private prisons, but it seems strange to want to own a company that lobbies to make sure filing your taxes is difficult.

It has been revealed that zscaler also offers a stickier product, in my opinion. Cybersecurity for any organization isn't a "nice to have"; it's absolutely crucial. I am not as convinced that Intuit's software is equally essential.

Now, let's take a look at the tape:.

In a recent development, zscaler stock has outperformed Intuit by more than 400 percentage points over the past decade or so. Intuit hasn't even managed to keep pace with the broader market, lagging behind the S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.81%) by about 90 percentage points in that time frame.

Industry observers note that zscaler did report a loss in its most recent fiscal year, but that figure is improving over time, and it's hard to argue with the stock's returns. Past performance is no indication of future results, of course, but Zscaler gets my vote for 2027 and beyond.

What You Can Pay for with Scholarship Money

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (840 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nerdwallet

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that scholarships are meant to pay for the cost of attendance to study at a college or university.
  • It has been revealed that some scholarships restrict the funds to specific costs, such as tuition.
  • Here are the most common college costs you can pay with scholarship money.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that scholarships are meant to pay for the cost of attendance to study at a college or university. This often includes required bills and purchases, such as tuition, textbooks and on-campus living expenses.

It has been revealed that some scholarships restrict the funds to specific costs, such as tuition. How you can apply the money may depend on the scholarship’s requirements.

Here are the most common college costs you can pay with scholarship money.

» MORE: Best websites for scholarships.

Scholarships commonly pay toward the tuition and fees your college charges.

Tuition usually covers only the cost to enroll in classes. Your college will also charge fees for a variety of reasons, such as attending a lab portion of a class, access to on-campus technology, facility maintenance and student activities. You’ll have to pay many of these fees regardless of if you use those facilities or participate in campus activities. Fees are often charged with tuition on the same bill so that you pay them together.

Industry observers note that tuition and fees cost students at public four-year institutions an average of $32,730 for the 2026-2027 school year, according to College Board’s 2026 report. If you use scholarship money to pay for these costs upfront, it can help you save a good chunk of money.

Recent findings suggest that scholarship money also pays for textbooks and supplies you need to complete your courses. These can include physical books, e-books and software licenses to access online content.

According to recent reports, depending on the scholarship, the cost of additional supplies that are required for certain courses might be covered as well. For example, nursing students might have to purchase scrubs with their college’s logo or medical supplies such as stethoscopes for clinical shifts.

Some scholarships will pay for the purchase of a laptop because you’ll likely need one to complete your coursework; however, you’ll want to confirm that the money can be used for that purchase before buying one.

Your scholarship might help cover some of the costs of living on campus, including paying for a dorm room and meal plans (often called room and board). To apply the funds, you usually have to live in university housing, which might be in a dormitory or even university apartments.

Sources indicate that many students can purchase meal plans to eat meals in their college and university cafeterias. These plans are usually for a set number of meals each week and might be required for first-year students. Because meal plans are part of college expenses, some scholarships will let you apply the funds to purchase a meal plan.

Some scholarships might also allow money to pay for campus parking fees because those are paid directly to the college or university.

» MORE: What is need-based financial aid for college?

It has been revealed that scholarships are generally intended only for educational expenses such as those explained above, but there are some scholarships that want you to use the money for specific expenses. If your scholarship has this type of restriction, your award letter should outline how the funds must be used, such as paying for tuition and fees only.

If you aren’t certain whether there are restrictions on how you can spend your scholarship money and the scholarship was paid directly to your college, you can call your financial aid office to ask. But you’ll want to contact the organization that awarded you the scholarship to ask about restrictions if the scholarship money was sent to you instead.

Even if a scholarship is open to most educational costs, expenses that are rarely allowed to be covered by a scholarship include:.

Some transportation costs such as car payments.

Non-essential supplies such as clothing or entertainment.

Travel, especially unrelated to college.

Scholarships can be paid directly to your college or to you, depending on the individual scholarship. If the money goes to your college, it’s applied to your account based on the scholarship’s requirements. For example, if the funds are only allowed to pay for tuition, the financial aid office will apply the money to your tuition bill to reduce how much you owe.

Scholarships work the same way for room and board. If your scholarship will pay toward the costs of living on campus, the money will reduce how much you owe or cover the costs entirely so that you don’t owe anything.

In some cases, you might be able to use your scholarship money to pay for books or supplies. If that’s allowed, the funds might be available on your account through the college bookstore. Instead of paying the entire cost of your textbooks with cash or your student loans, you can pay with the scholarship money.

If your scholarship sends you the money instead of giving it to your college, you’ll be responsible for using the funds to pay for eligible costs instead of your university automatically applying it toward your bill.

According to recent reports, independent oil and natural gas firm Permian Resources (PR) is this week's first dividend stock. The company recently paid a quarterly base cash dividend of 16 cents per share. At an annualized dividend of 64 cents per share, PR offers a dividend yield of 3.5%.

It has been revealed that recently, Evercore analyst Chris Baker initiated coverage of Permian Resources stock with a price target of $25. The analyst believes that the firm is well positioned to benefit from improving U.S. shale demand after the Iran conflict, thanks to its low-breakeven inventory that can boost free cash flow growth. Baker also noted PR's disciplined consolidation in the Permian Basin.

Furthermore, the 5-star analyst highlighted the company's focus on a single basin and management's efficient capital allocations across expansion efforts, strategic acquisitions, and share buybacks. Baker noted that management focuses investments on the higher-return Northern Delaware Basin, helping boost profitability.

"The key piece of our work here, and the reason we think PR deserves a higher multiple relative to more finite or less flexible shale stories, is that PR runs an acquire and exploit model," remarked Baker.

He explained that Permian Resources deserves a premium valuation as it continually acquires and develops fresh high-quality assets instead of relying on a limited inventory, a strategy that is the market is underappreciating.

Baker ranks No. 862 among more than 12,300 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 75% of the time, delivering an average return of 48.3%. See Permian Resources Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

Valero Energy (VLO) is a manufacturer and marketer of petroleum-based and low-carbon liquid transportation fuels and petrochemical products. At a quarterly dividend of $1.20 per share, or annualized dividend of $4.80 per share, VLO stock offers a yield of about 2%.

Heading into Valero's second-quarter earnings on July 30, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reiterated a buy rating on VLO stock and increased the price target to $286 from $283 to reflect updated estimates.

Moving on to Ovintiv (OVV), a North American oil and natural gas producer. It has solid positions in North America's premier oil basins – the Permian and the Montney. OVV offers a quarterly dividend of 30 cents per share, or an annualized dividend of $1.20 per share, implying a 2.3% yield.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Ben Gran – Nov 19, 2026 at 6:34AM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Vanguard Morningstar Total Stock Market ETF ›.

It has been revealed that I've been investing in stocks since 2004, when I left my first job in the public sector and moved to a corporate employer with a 401(k) blueprint. I had some money from cashing out my unvested public sector pension. And I had saved up a few thousand dollars to put into a Roth IRA.

I was in my mid-20s and I didn't know what I was doing. The stock market in those days didn't seem real to me. I wasn't a sophisticated investor. But I knew I wanted to save for the future, and that putting money into tax-advantaged accounts and investing in stocks was, in general, the right move for someone like me to make.

The stock market was pretty calm in the first few years of my investing life. Here were the annual stock market returns from the S&P 500 index (^GSPC +0.81%) during those years:.

Data source: S&P historical annual returns, Macrotrends.net.

But then 2008 hit. My first bear market was a bad one. Here's what happened to the S&P 500 in 2008:.

Let's look at what I learned from my first bear market -- and how that significant investing lesson still inspires my decisions today.

This wasn't my first rodeo. I had graduated from college in 2001 and lived through the dot-com bust and the Enron scandal. But the 2008 global financial crisis and Great Recession were much more severe and affected the entire economy. And on a personal level, 2008 was much scarier than 2001.

That's because by 2008, I had some skin in the game. I had a job at a major bank. I had become more established in my career and as an investor. I had built up a few years' worth of savings in my 401(k) and Roth IRA. My wife and I had a baby and a mortgage. We were just trying to have a happy little life with a home, family, friends, and some financial stability for the future. And all of a sudden, it seemed like the housing market, the stock market, and the entire financial system were on the brink of collapse.

In a recent development, all bad things seemed possible in 2008. Would I lose my job? Would we lose our house?

It's strange to think back on it now, because while 2008 was happening, I could barely focus on the stock market. Banks were failing and the market was crashing, but I was too worried about holding onto my job. I just wanted to keep paying the bills, putting food on the table, and taking care of our baby. I wasn't making clever moves like buying more stocks when prices were low. I was just trying to hold on to what we had.

Industry observers note that perhaps the biggest lesson from my first bear market is: I am incredibly lucky. I never lost my job in 2008. We never missed a mortgage payment. The bank that I worked for did not go out of business; it actually emerged from the financial crisis stronger than ever, unlike other major banks and subprime lenders that failed during the housing crash.

But being lucky is not an actionable lesson for investors. It's good to be lucky. But it's even better to have a strategy and stick with it. So the real big lesson from my first bear market is: Keep buying stocks. As long as you have a job, as long as you have steady income, try to keep putting some money into the stock market as often as you can. Every month, every payday.

Recent findings suggest that I never stopped buying stocks in 2008. I kept investing in my 401(k) plan every month, every payday, with dollar-cost averaging. I kept putting cash into my Roth IRA, even when money was tight. Those simple, steady, disciplined, "boring" little investments might end up being some of the most lucrative financial moves I've ever made in my life.

According to recent reports, since those crisis-era lows of 2008, the stock market has skyrocketed with a long, mostly uninterrupted bull market. A $1,000 investment in the S&P 500 at the end of 2008 would have grown to almost $8,400 today.

At this point in my life, I try to stay calm and unbothered during major swings in the stock market. Hopefully, 2008 will be the worst economic crisis of my lifetime. But even if there is another terrible short-term crisis like 2008, I know that in the long run, the S&P 500 is likely to bounce back.

Buying low-cost index funds like the Vanguard Morningstar Total Stock Market ETF (VTI +0.93%) tends to be a great move for people with a long-term time horizon, even if you end up buying stocks at "the wrong time" right before a crash.

NYSEMKT · As of 9:41 AM ET 11/19/26.

This total stock market ETF is a big part of my portfolio. It holds 3,511 U.S. stocks of all sectors and sizes, from the S&P 500 to small caps. Even if there is a tech stock crash or a big sell-off in artificial intelligence (AI) stocks soon, I believe that in the long run, index funds like the Vanguard Morningstar Total Stock Market ETF will eventually recover and rebalance. VTI lets me own the future "winners" of the economy, one way or another.

That's why I keep buying stocks. Even when the market is crashing, when investor fear is rampant, when the headlines are full of doom. I've lived through worse. And in the long run, the stock market tends to go up. If you keep buying during the lowest points of a bear market, when stocks are cheapest, your investments will slingshot upward as the market rises in the future.

How Silicon Valley lost the public, with Crooked Media’s Jon Favreau
