💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Crooked Media cofounder on why material conditions beat the billionaire-owned media, and what a Democratic Congress should do about AI.
  • Today, I’m talking with Jon Favreau, a political commentator and cofounder of Crooked Media.
  • Since then, Pod Save America and the company created around it, Crooked, have become one of the major success stories of independent liberal media.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Crooked Media cofounder on why material conditions beat the billionaire-owned media, and what a Democratic Congress should do about AI.

Today, I’m talking with Jon Favreau, a political commentator and cofounder of Crooked Media. You probably know Jon best from a little show called Pod Save America, which Jon started with a group of fellow Obama staffers in the wake of Donald Trump’s election in 2016. It’s now one of the most popular podcasts in the country.

Since then, Pod Save America and the company created around it, Crooked, have become one of the major success stories of independent liberal media. So one of my central questions for Jon was why he thought Democrats swept the midterms earlier this month and, more importantly, why it happened now — especially after a wave of tech billionaires made big swings to the right while buying huge pillars of the information ecosystem.

Recent findings suggest that that’s Elon Musk buying Twitter and turning it into X, Mark Zuckerberg sucking up to Trump while tearing down Meta’s content moderation infrastructure, the Ellison family buying stakes in TikTok, turning over the leadership of CBS News and now potentially CNN while integrating Warner into Skydance… the list goes on. How did they all miss the huge swing in the mood of the public — or, more apocalyptically, fail in their attempts to control the media and thus influence the public?

According to recent reports, crooked itself is also just a fascinating business, as all creator businesses are. When we think of what you might call news creators, we tend to look to the right — after all, conservative media have been building an alternative, direct-to-consumer pipeline since the dawn of talk radio.

But Jon and his fellow Crooked cofounders created a reliable template for liberal creators, and it’s working. Crooked hired its first CEO a few years ago, now offers more than a dozen original indicates, and has a staff of around 100 people working on everything from live events to political advocacy. Jon tells me the subscription business has crossed 65,000 members.

So of course I wanted to know how Jon feels about topics we cover a lot here on Decoder: online distribution, the platform power of YouTube, and how you balance running a media business that has to make money with a newsroom that, ultimately, has a political mission and a strong point of view.

Industry observers note that of course, AI. Jon has turned his own podcast Offline into something close to an AI policy show this year. He has a lot of thoughts on how Congress should tackle the matter.

Okay: Jon Favreau, the co-host of Pod Save America and cofounder of Crooked Media. Here we go.

This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Jon Favreau, you’re the co-host of Pod Save America, you’re the host of Offline. You’re also the co-founder of Crooked Media. Welcome to Decoder.

In a recent development, I’m excited to have you here. I’ve been on Offline with you. It was a really fun conversation.

I have a million ideas about what to talk about with you. I want to talk about Crooked as a creator tech giant in this particular moment in media. I feel like we have to start with the midterms though. The blue tsunami is here. It feels like a repudiation of the billionaires owning all the social platforms, the billionaires owning all the broadcast networks.

In a recent development, what do you make of that? I’ve just been turning this over in my head that the media was purchased in a huge and meaningful way, and Americans stated, “No, we still see through it.”.

I think it’s a repudiation of a government that came into power with the chief promise of bringing inflation down and making life more affordable, and it didn’t do that. If you’ve looked at the last couple of elections, people voted a party into power and they mentioned, “Everything’s too expensive and I want stuff to be cheaper and I don’t want to be struggling. Can you do something about it?”.

And then either they try to do something about it or they fail to do something about it or like Trump, you don’t even try at all. You actually make life harder, and then people say, “The propaganda that’s coming out of Fox or any of these right-wing platforms doesn’t matter. I fill up my car and gas is expensive and I don’t know if I’m ever going to be able to afford a house because interest rates are up, et cetera, et cetera.”.

You can say whatever you want to say, but people’s lived experiences end up being more salient than the messages that they get from politics.

It’s just, “Gas prices are up, just throw the bums out.” But I would say the last 10 years of politics are, “Can I tweak policy into reality?” We’ve seen it happen several times. “Can I wage memetic warfare on the American public until these Republican talking points are the framework in which all further conversation must happen?”.

We’ve seen it happen on the left too. I think Defund the Police is a great example of a thing that just spiraled out of control and maybe turned an election. But in particular, we’re going to wake up and the Fox News machine is going to define the terms of the debate, and then we’re going to wake up and whatever’s happening on Twitter is going to define the terms of the debate. That has been how it’s worked for an awfully long time, and “the gas prices are too high” and “this war is stupid” maybe just defeated it.

It works to a point, but there are certain conditions that messaging and media just can’t overcome, especially for the party in power or forever, whoever’s running the White House.

According to recent reports, the same was true with Joe Biden. Joe Biden could go out there and say, “We passed this bill. We gave money out. We gave the checks out and things are getting better and we’re just recovering from Covid. You haven’t felt it yet, but it’s getting better and look at the economic statistics.” And people just noted, “No, I don’t feel that yet. So I’m going to maybe give Donald Trump another try, even though I think he’s a shitty guy and I don’t like him very much.” But maybe they remember the economy of the first term being good.

We dealt with this when Obama ran and became president in 2009. They thought, “Financial crisis. Can’t stand Bush anymore. I’m going to try Obama.” And then Obama gets into office and for the first two years, the financial crisis is over, but the recession is still there. People are still out of work.

So they mentioned, “I know you passed healthcare and I know you passed the recovery act, but I still can’t find a job. The economy just still doesn’t feel great to me. So it doesn’t matter what you say you did or how great your messaging is, I don’t feel it. I’m going to vote in a Republican Congress.” It’s been like that for as long as I’ve been in politics.

It has been revealed that is there some reason the incumbent party does not realize that saying something that sounds like “the fundamentals of the economy are strong” kills you? Because you’re describing a pattern that repeats and it’s that phrase almost exactly.

Recent findings suggest that yes. That’s why we understood it once 2012 rolled around because people were still not satisfied with the economy when Obama was running for reelection and we did everything we could to make that election a choice. We acknowledged that people were still struggling and people were still in pain. We totally avoided the long list of statistics about how wonderful the economy was getting and how everyone had recovered and all that kind of stuff. We just noted, “Look, things are still rough out there, but it’s a choice. This is the kind of vision Mitt Romney has for the economy and this is the vision we have for the economy. You get to pick one.”.

It has been revealed that there’s a way, if you are the incumbent party in power, to still keep people on your side, but you’ve got to at least acknowledge and be honest about how people are feeling. You can’t tell people to feel a way that they aren’t feeling. You can’t tell people that a whole bunch of issues are important that aren’t the issues that matter most to them in their lives or at least to most people, which is, “Do I feel economically secure and do I actually feel safe?” That’s why people care about crime and they care about safety in their communities and then they also care about whether they can afford gas and groceries.

Sources indicate that the one issue that really struck me in that framework is surveillance. We’ve done a number of episodes about Flock cameras and AI-enabled surveillance and the idea that you can just link all the databases together and Palantir can send a drone to your house to murder you. That connects directly to safety.

According to recent reports, the CEO of Ring has been on the show and his argument is, “If I put up enough Ring cameras, I will zero out crime in certain neighborhoods.” I’ve asked him about the mechanism of how that will exactly work and the answer is that the thieves will be deterred by surveillance. It’s the same for the CEO of Flock. It’s the same argument everywhere. “If we just watch you enough, we’ll stop crime.” The American public hates this idea. There’s some limit to how much crime-stopping you want compared to how much surveillance must occur.

I watched the CEO of Flock in particular try to go hard MAGA in this election cycle and use the phrase, “The radical leftists want a crime world,” or whatever it is he was saying, and it just didn’t work. That to me felt like a glimmer of a realignment where the libertarians in America were saying, “No, we still don’t want a state with this level of power,” and your classic ACLU Democrats were saying, “Yep, that’s pretty bad,” and then throw all the bumps out, like, “Just get out of here and we’ll start over.”.

It has been revealed that what do you make of that? Because there are other glimmers of realignment, but that is the one that really stuck out to me.

It’s interesting. I do think privacy is the other matter that affects people personally, that they can feel. You go through your life and if you lose your privacy, then there’s public shaming and embarrassment — there’s a violation there.

Recent findings suggest that so at least in people’s minds, they still do balance safety and security with privacy concerns. We have that in so many aspects of life. But you see with the Flock cameras, that’s also why Trump’s immigration policy has gone so poorly for them politically, because you have the same voters who say, “I think the border was a bit of a mess under Biden,” and even people who are welcoming to immigrants say, “I think there’s too many immigrants all at once coming over the border.” We didn’t know what to do. Public services were strained, especially in some of these border communities.

The same people who wanted a more secure border suddenly looked around and said, “I also don’t want the government with masked, armed federal agents coming into my community and kidnapping people and taking them off the street and having that fear as I go about my day that I may be taken by the state just because of what I look like or how I talk or who I’m associated with. Or if I’m trying to protest the government, which is my constitutional right, then they might come after me then too.”.

It’s too early to tell if it’s a realignment, but I do think there’s this resistance to state power, or state overreach, that we haven’t seen the extent of in another administration in our lifetime, that is as bad as it’s been with Donald Trump in his second term.

It is also that privacy, to some huge extent, is actually a free speech and First Amendment [glitch]. We’ve seen this with FCC Chairman Brendan Carr. I keep calling him a dummy. I get all these notes saying, “Why do you call him dummy? He’s evil.” I’m saying, “No, because he’s dumb. This is strategically dumb. Fighting comedians is stupid. This is bad. Both sides will turn on him the second he doesn’t have a Donald Trump to protect him.”.

In a recent development, I think we’re going to see it. There are incoming members of Congress talking about FCC oversight today. But that one felt like another glimmer of, “Oh, this one party has gone too far. They own all the channels of speech. We are watching Elon Musk turn the moderation knobs however he wants it and the chairman of the FCC is attacking comedians. We don’t have to overthink this. We can just call this bad.”.

The third one is AI. It’s data centers where you see both sides coming together to say no. Something like 41 of 43 data center moratoriums passed. And that’s just classic American NIMBYism: “I just don’t want this loud building here.” What do you make of that one?

Industry observers note that it’s classic American NIMBYism, but it’s also this larger feeling that we’re losing control of the forces that shape our lives. Because when you talk to people who oppose the data centers, so much of it is about, “There was an NDA. It was all a secret. We couldn’t express our opposition to this before the deal was already done.”.

Part of it is connected to AI. Part of it is just, “My electricity bills are going up. It’s fucking noisy.” Any of the people who live around data centers, it’s unbelievably noisy. It’s bright in the middle of the night. In some cases, you see communities where the community has gotten together and stated, “I don’t want a data center,” and the local politicians say they don’t want it and they get overruled and somehow the data center ends up there anyway. At least there’s been a turn there and that’s not happening as much anymore.

But I do think there’s this feeling that, “We don’t want this in our community and yet more powerful companies and politicians are shoving it down our throats anyway, and we’re not going to take that because we should have control over what happens in our lives and what happens in our community.”.

According to recent reports, we did a big story on Kevin O’Leary’s project in Utah. We reported it out and we were there. And we assumed he would talk to us because he talks to everybody. We got to the end and we sent our “no surprises” email and he sent his lawyers back at us and I thought, “Thank you for this incredible gift of threatening us.”.

Threatening us with legal action for talking to people in Utah about his data center. But that’s the level of aggression that most of these big projects come with.

Meta really loves talking about its project in Louisiana, but it doesn’t feel like the people in Louisiana felt like that was a choice they made. That was something Meta imposed on them and now the teachers got a raise and they need to be quiet.

They don’t feel the need to explain the projects or the data centers to the community. Even the people who are very pro-data centers say, “There are a lot of conspiracy theories about data centers and all this opposition is based in propaganda. Actually you can build them so that they run on clean energy and that they pay for the power.”.

In a recent development, all of this might be true, but the companies — the hyperscalers, Meta and all these places that are trying to build these data centers — didn’t bother to try to explain the benefits. They didn’t bother to try to tell people in advance that this was happening or negotiate with communities. They’re doing it all now because of the pushback.

Recent findings suggest that but at the time, it was more, “You say that this is going to go great for us, but you also stated social media was going to go great for us.” If you just look at the larger economy with AI, people said globalization was going to go great for people. People are tired of hearing from people in elite circles, whether it’s in business or government, who say, “This fresh technological advance in development is going to be great for everyone. Trust us and just let us do what we want and you’ll benefit at some point.” People just say, “No, I don’t trust you anymore.”.

Industry observers note that yeah, it’s funny. My hottest take continues to be that if consumer AI products were any good, these companies would have an easier time. Google’s AI overviews are not good enough to convince anyone to build a data center. Deepfake slop on Instagram is not going to convince anyone to build a data center.

The best pitch they have is, “One day we’ll cure cancer,” but you might still have to navigate the healthcare system for that to happen to you. That seems pretty opaque. And then it’s like Salesforce will get better and an ultra-weaponized B2B SaaS environment is not going to do it.

According to recent reports, if you just put the Netflix logo on the side of the data center, people might calm down. They like Netflix, but there’s no consumer product that is making the sale. It’s just these guys and they don’t seem capable of doing it.

No. And they continue to sit down for interviews and say, “Yeah, and it could kill everyone and it could do all that, but also there’s plenty of good that’s coming from it and we’ve got it covered. We’ve got it covered.”.

So to wrap this all up — and then I want to talk about Crooked and I want to talk about where we go from here — the thing that I was thinking about as I watched the election returns come in was at the beginning of Trump 2.0, there was a Steve Bannon quote that just ricocheted through my mind in our coverage. It was “politics is downstream of culture.“ This is just the [Breitbart] thesis.

Recent findings suggest that I tend to believe Steve Bannon on this actually, that the cultural atmosphere of the country has some big effect on our politics. And then I watched the Trump administration engineer the sale or control of TikTok to Oracle and Larry Ellison. I watched CBS News get taken over by the Ellisons and Bari Weiss. I watched Elon Musk turn the knobs on X even harder. I watched the FCC work its way towards the removal of the restriction on broadcast ownership, so even fewer big companies could own more broadcast stations in the country.

According to recent reports, I thought, “Oh, the mechanisms of culture are bending their will to the Trump administration and this is going to lead to some permanent political outcome.” We covered it that way. Then this election happened, and that appears to have been totally wrong. I just got that wrong and I’m still trying to figure that out.

Politics is downstream from culture, but material conditions rule out. As you are trying to form an opposition to the incumbent party — whatever it may be, and now it’s the Trump administration — culture is important to bringing people onto your side and building a movement and building an opposition that’s powerful enough to defeat the current incumbents. That’s going to be important.

But in terms of whether you are the incumbent and whether you are the party in power and material conditions aren’t great, ultimately it doesn’t matter if you control the culture, or at least it doesn’t help you as much as people think it might because you can’t outrun material conditions.

Industry observers note that I wonder if that’s going to lead to a Woke 3.0. A former Verge reporter, Kylie Robison, tweeted at Jason Calacanis, “Put the pronouns in bio lil bro,” which is just one of the funniest reposts on election night that I saw.

I’m wondering, do you think that there is a cultural pendulum swing coming, or is it straightforwardly “improve our material conditions”?

Now, this could end up being naive, but I think that the left has grown over the decade and learned from the excesses of Woke 1.0.

Industry observers note that did I say Woke 3.0? I meant Woke 2.0.

[Laughs] Woke 2.0. My staff mentioned this too. They were talking about Woke 3.0 and I said, “Guys, what happened to Woke 2.0?”.

In a recent development, woke 2.0 is crypto. We don’t talk about that.

I was asking them, “Where did Woke 2.0 go?” But, no, I do think that there’s tons of factional fighting in the Democratic Party as there always is.

But there does seem to be broad agreement on making sure that the party focuses on people’s material conditions and affordability. You even see that acknowledgement on the right as well. JD Vance said that, Ted Cruz said that. So it’s on the mind of all the people who are going to run for president in 2028.

The left is very cognizant, especially progressives, of what the culture wars and woke and all that kind of stuff cost them, fairly or unfairly. They don’t want to make that mistake again. Because I think everyone on the left, from the far left to the center left, understands the stakes in a way that we might not have when Trump first took office in 2016.

Industry observers note that I want to come back to that as we talk about the future of the media ecosystem, but this is a good place to talk about Crooked itself. You started Crooked in the Trump administration. It’s a product of the first Trump administration. It has grown to become a force. I have here in my notes that some people call you a kingmaker. It’s an honor to be in your presence.

[Laughs] What king have we made?

Sources indicate that if you could make me one, that would be great. I think I’d be an excellent king of America. Tell me about Crooked. How is this tech giant structured? How does it work?

We started in 2016 as a podcast. When we were in the White House, Tommy Vietor, Jon Lovett and I had talked about how there’s not enough progressive media out there. Part of it is because people in progressive media, just like people in politics, take themselves too seriously. There’s not a lot of joking around because everything is “end of the world” kind of stuff.

According to recent reports, we have Vote Save America, which is the advocacy arm of the company. It just raised a couple million dollars for this last cycle and asked people to run for office themselves who listened to the show. We had 2,000 people raise their hands to run for office this last cycle. A bunch of them won. Part of the theory when we started is we don’t want to just tell people what’s broken about the world, but give them the tools and information they need to fix it. There was advocacy built into the founding of the company.

According to recent reports, but somewhere around 2022, we finally decided that we need a CEO for this organization. We need a real grownup. So we hired Lucinda Treat to be our CEO in 2022, and it has let the three of us focus on editorial and making content. Lucinda runs the company, and that has been a real blessing. Because running a company of 100 people is not something I’m good at, I would say.

Yeah, I run a newsroom of like 50 and I’m still figuring it out every day. So 100 people, 16 podcasts — how is that basically organized? What’s the general structure there?

Sources indicate that lucinda is the CEO, and under her we have a head of news and politics and a head of culture and entertainment. Just as every organization has, we have finance and marketing, and people and culture. Vote Save America is headquartered in DC, and we have a few news folks in DC. We have some newsletters as well, because we’re on Substack now.

According to recent reports, we have two reporters who are in DC and covering stuff there. Now we’re expanding. We just launched Still Counting with Nate Silver, Clare Malone and Galen Druke, which is a reboot of FiveThirtyEight, and they’re in Fresh York. So we now have a presence in New York as well.

Sources indicate that we’re in a real moment for creator-led media. You’re describing a group of three creators who expanded and have more people making content. There’s a business operation around you. You have a newsroom. You’re creators with a newsroom. That is fundamentally what I’m hearing. Maybe I’m getting that wrong, but it sounds like you’re creators with the newsroom.

Somewhere in there is, “We have to find new people to pay for a subscription, and we need new people to listen to the podcast.” All of that discovery happens on someone else’s platform. That is the real dynamic for every creator, right? We need to invest in YouTube. At any moment, YouTube could turn the knobs, just as Elon turned the knobs on X. How do you feel about that? How do you manage that pressure?

It’s just the reality, and so we have to go with it. It’s funny, because when we look at the RSS feed, which is where regular old audio podcasts are—.

[Laughs] Everyone’s perfect RSS feed.

Recent findings suggest that I do think YouTube has been a wonderful growth opportunity because it’s much harder to grow the actual audio RSS feed. But to your point, the fact that we’re all dependent on a YouTube algorithm is not great. The only solution for that is to just be on as many platforms as possible, and to be everywhere all at once.

Do you find that the revenue opportunities on all those platforms equal out? Did some rise and some fall, or do you have a more lucrative one?

According to recent reports, the podcast ad market is still the bread and butter, just because it’s more reliable and sustainable. YouTube monetization is catching up now. But most of our revenue is still from the ads and the podcast stuff.

According to recent reports, one of the most accidentally rude things I find myself saying about the creator industry is that everyone has to run a little ad agency. That substantial creators are better described as little ad agencies than whatever it is that they thought they were doing.

I say it’s accidentally rude because I don’t begrudge anyone running a business. It’s very difficult to run a media company. Please go and succeed. But when you’re running a little ad agency, sometimes it just comes through that you’re running a little ad agency. There’s a whole suite of tech creators and AI creators where I think it’s coming through more clearly than ever before. There are some that are very good, and like everything, there’s a wide range.

In a recent development, you explicitly have an advocacy arm. Does that make it easier to do the advertising? Does that make it easier to have that point of view? I find it very challenging.

Industry observers note that there are just a lot of advertisers that we won’t work with. There are a lot of advertisers who won’t work with us because of our political affiliation.

Black Rifle Coffee isn’t coming to your doorstep?

The more explicitly partisan and political the podcast, the fewer advertisers you have, at least the bigger blue chip ones that want to get involved in politics. But then for us, there are a lot of companies and a lot of products where we think, “Does that conflict with our values?” And if it does….

We have these conversations all the time. We don’t just take whoever to be our advertisers. That makes it a little bit trickier. But there’s also plenty of advertising we do for causes and campaigns and stuff like that. I guess we make it up a little bit there. But it can be more challenging.

According to recent reports, one of the ideas that I’ve just been turning around in my head as I’ve been talking to more and more creators lately is that the value of the creator advertising is actually in what you say no to. I know big creators who could say yes to everything and they say, “No, I don’t want to do it. My audience would be upset if I did this.”.

Whereas, if you work at a media company, on the other side of the firewall there’s a group of people whose job it is to say yes. And you’re saying, “Well, I guess we’re doing that today. I had nothing to do with it.”.

According to recent reports, our young audience does not actually understand that wall exists. I find myself explaining this hundred-year-old journalism tradition all the time. Because in the creator world it just doesn’t exist, and you are making those choices all the time. How does that express itself? You stated you have these conversations. What does that actually look like?

There are certain categories of ads that we have to think about, like banks. Do we want to be advertising for significant banks? Do we want to be advertising for any company or product or service which is explicitly against our political values? We dealt with this a lot earlier too, which is then you have to look at the company and say, “Is it a perfect company? Has it had complaints?”.

Sources indicate that at some point you can’t be looking at every single complaint about the manufacturer as a reason to not advertise for that company. Drawing the lines is not a perfect process. It’s necessarily ad hoc, which is why even though the three of us are mainly focused on editorial and content, we will still take a look at the advertisers coming on, or at least it’ll come to us if they may be controversial. And then we have to have a conversation about that.

One of my friends, who is a tech writer, has the point of view, “I will accept money from everyone except the seven most successful companies in the history of the world,” which is just not an economical way of thinking about it, but that’s the line. “All right, I’m just not going to take massive tech money because I need to talk about them all the time.”.

And it’s tough because also major tech money and crypto, and the betting markets, are the big advertisers these days.

Would you do a Kalshi integration?

Sources indicate that not for Pod Save America, no. We have deals with hosts who are independent contractors, and so if a host came to us and said they wanted to do one, we could talk about it. But not for Pod Save America. I wouldn’t do it for Offline either. I just think the betting on politics... First of all, I’m in the camp that doesn’t think prediction markets for politics are that useful. They mostly reflect conventional wisdom, and oftentimes conventional wisdom is right. It often isn’t.

The idea that the prediction markets, at least around politics, have this very special insight into what’s going to happen that polls can’t offer you has not been proven out to me yet.

There’s a part of the whole prediction market dynamic where eventually they will have to admit that the markets are only predictive if they have illegal inside trading in them.

Like that’s the only way they can actually be predictive.

It has been revealed that the reason I’m asking this is I think we’re going to enter an era where creator businesses are more ascendant than ever. We saw the takeover of the platforms not be effective. We saw the takeover of the broadcast media not necessarily be effective. Fox News doesn’t seem all that effective.

It’s going to be this — it’s going to be creators on platforms talking directly to audiences about material conditions and how that not just remains sustainable, but grows to meet the ambition you might have, other creators might have, and also the demand for audiences.

Somewhere in there you run out of saying, “We’re just an ad agency.” You have to diversify and you have to do subscriptions. You have to find other lines of business. You might have to consolidate. How are you thinking about that growth? Or is that just Lucinda’s job?

Recent findings suggest that that is mostly Lucinda’s job. But we want to take substantial bets on highlights. It is interesting, because we know that our audience comes to us for politics and political analysis. So when we launch new shows, it doesn’t mean that every show we launch has to be all about politics, but it still has to appeal to our audience or audiences that would say, “Okay, it makes sense to come to Crooked to listen to this.”.

Jon Lovett has Lovett or Leave It, which is his comedy show. It works really well because Lovett has political experience and all the jokes are about politics. That makes sense as a Crooked product. It’s the same thing with Nate Silver’s pod, which was a natural acquisition for us because our audience loves getting into the weeds on numbers.

Alex Wagner came to us and she has a pod, Runaway Country, also a natural fit. Then the question for us as we expand is, from a content perspective, “How can we grow the type of content that we offer audiences while not going so far afield from what our core business is that people would not come to us first versus another competitor or somewhere else that does entertainment or culture or tech better than we do?” That’s usually the thought process we go through as we’re trying to figure out how to grow.

It has been revealed that I feel like I should have asked you the other Decoder question because we’re in the weeds of it. But the other Decoder question I ask everybody is: How do you make decisions? What’s your framework for that?

According to recent reports, it’s funny, we have this whole other lens here, which is how to influence the political debate. At least for me, that’s the most important thing. We’ve now built a successful business that yes, I want to see grow. It also chugs along nicely on its own right now.

When there is a debate between whether we want to do something that’s going to make us more money or whether we want to do something that we think is going to move along the debate in politics, we choose the latter. At least I choose the latter. A lot of the guys want to as well.

We want to be influential in the political debate. It’s partly because of what you just mentioned about the media environment, where there are so many different sources of information now that I think from a political perspective, it’s really difficult to get a message out to the electorate that everyone hears the same.

We’re not in the world where everyone’s going to watch the nightly news. When I was on the Obama campaign in ‘08, we knew that whatever events he did, we would judge the success of them through the prism of the three nightly news networks. That worked out pretty well for us as a campaign, even though we were on Facebook and trying to organize people on Facebook and do all that stuff back then.

According to recent reports, the way you judged the success of an event in a day was, “How did it play on the evening news?” That world is long gone. From the perspective of how we keep democracy together so that everyone is getting good, reliable information and that everyone is debating the same information, that’s just a really, really hard task. I see our job as trying to make that a little easier for people, at least on our side, on the left side of the political spectrum.

We want to be a place where people on the far left, people on the center left, Never Trumpers and people on the right can at least feel comfortable coming on, debating, talking to us because we’re trying to reconnect the civic discussion that has been just completely balkanized over the last 10 years.

It has been revealed that my favorite example of what you’re describing is Zohran Mamdani. I don’t think he’s ever answered a question without saying he loves New York City in the same way that Dr. Pimple Popper is always like, “I’m a dermatologist.” Literally just saying the first fact, reading his LinkedIn, because he can’t assume that you have any idea what’s going on. So “I love New York City” is just the first fact and then whatever answer. It comes up every single time.

Sources indicate that that is partially an algorithmic problem. It’s partially just a media fragmentation problem. But you’re describing something bigger than that. You’re describing a shared value system. We might have different political ideas or different policy prescriptions, but we will agree that the Strait of Hormuz is closed.

According to recent reports, we’re going to start there. That requires you to fight the algorithm. It requires you to fight the filter bubble. How do you take that approach? Are you just saying you love Upcoming York City over and over again or is there something else?

You try to appear in a bunch of different information streams. You try to be on a whole bunch of different platforms. You try to go on a bunch of different demonstrates. You try to have people on with all kinds of different perspectives from different parts of the political spectrum, just so that you’re cross-pollinating more with different audiences. That’s really notable. We think about that as one strategy.

But beyond that, it’s really difficult. People bemoan the demise of monoculture, and I think it’s not just a problem for entertainment and culture, or whatever it may be. It’s the biggest problem for politics. If there are no events, shows, or moments in time where everyone in the country is focused on the same thing, consuming the same information, and consuming the same entertainment, that’s a problem for a society that needs to govern itself. I don’t think there’s a good solution for that, but that is something that at least we think about while we’re making decisions.

The other viewpoint on this is actually Bari Weiss. I saw her do an interview with Jessica Lessin of The information a couple weeks ago and Bari’s argument is the media lost trust. It lost everyone’s trust by miscovering all this stuff and she thinks she needs to tear this down and rebuild it for the lost middle.

You can look at CBS’s ratings and decide whether or not that has been effective, but I hear that argument all the time — that this is actually a trust problem, that the media is lying to you. You can go online and you’ll hear the real truth about whatever it is. What do you make of that argument? What do you make of Bari Weiss making that argument?

According to recent reports, she’s right in that all of this is fundamentally a trust problem, but it’s not just a loss of trust in liberal media or what she would call liberal media. It’s a loss of trust in institutions across the board and across the political spectrum. It is fundamental to the rise of Donald Trump in the first place. We are now a low-trust society, even compared to other wealthy societies around the world.

It has been revealed that you go to Scandinavia and these are much higher-trust societies. They handled Covid better. They handled the pandemic better because of that. America’s a very low-trust society. The balkanization of the media is a huge part of that. Even if you believe in one media institution, there’s another media institution that’s a competitor trying to tear that one down that’s going to tell you that they’re lying to you.

The number of people I’ve talked to, and I also see this in focus groups all the time, where people will say, “I listen to Fox News and I watch Fox News and I also watch MS Now because I have to get both sides now.” People are now trying to seek out more partisan viewpoints or political viewpoints in order to make the judgments for themselves, which is a tough place to put individuals in. But because there’s so little trust in media in general, but also in the government and corporations, that’s what people are left to do.

There was a report last year in Semafor that you had held talks with The Bulwark to discuss a partnership. Obviously The Bulwark started as a bunch of Never Trumpers. Is that enough expansion? You’re going to have a shared set of facts and probably some different policy prescriptions?

The thing with The Bulwark is because they’re just so like-minded to us, we like doing a lot of stuff with them. Whether it makes sense as a business partnership you can put aside, because of the amount of cross-pollination between our indicates. I’m always on Tim Miller’s podcast and he’s doing something with Lovett and Sarah Longwell’s doing something with Dan Pfeiffer.

We think that by doing more stuff with them, their audience is exposed to us, our audience is exposed to them, and that just helps with our larger political mission. We see it more as a political alliance and partnership than it is a business partnership.

Sources indicate that the reason I’m asking this is I see the creator businesses getting bigger. You can see the creators raising money to do roll-ups. I think Johnny Harris is raising money to roll up more YouTube channels. Right next to that is the platforms that hate this idea. The platforms would prefer the army of teenagers working for free.

In a recent development, the army of teenagers working for free never show up at YouTube’s door and say, “We would like better terms. We would like higher ad rates or we will withdraw our content.” It’s just, “We’re going to make more teenagers. You can leave.” We’ve seen this happen many times. Right now, something in the media ecosystem like Netflix is paying for podcasts and YouTube wants those people to stay.

There’s something where the creator media has gravity. It has real audience, that audience is durable, and going from YouTube to Netflix might actually harm YouTube in some way. Whatever is happening there seems crucial. How do you think about Crooked in that dynamic? Would you ever go to YouTube and say, “We’re going to leave you for Netflix?”.

I have to say, once a bunch of podcasts were on Netflix and I started taking a spin through Netflix, I thought, “Even with the algorithm there, it’s really tricky to find those podcasts on Netflix.” Now, if you just have a really popular podcast and you have an audience, then that’s great.

Industry observers note that but I just think that, at least from my perspective, it’s just easier to find your content on YouTube than it is on Netflix. I don’t think the money would be more valuable than the audience growth that you’d get on YouTube.

Recent findings suggest that to bring this all back around, I’ve heard you say these midterms represent the end of the Trump era. Whatever this was, it was blissfully over. All the politicians are now influencers unto themselves. JD Vance is a creature of X, for better or worse. That is how that man communicates. Mamdani is a creature of TikTok. The House Oversight Committee made what can only be described as an NBA hype reel about lawyering up.

Something has happened to our politics where this is how we communicate now. As you noted, the Democrats are a massive tent. They have a lot of differing priorities. We’ll see how that all gets expressed. What do you think happens now? Do you think they will be able to effectively communicate in the platform environment, in the media environment that we find ourselves in now?

That’s going to be difficult over the next two years. You still need a president, you need a leader of the party, to be able to try to effectively communicate. The Democrats who were successful on Election Day, which are most of the ones who are running [in 2028], were successful because they were their own little creator economies in their campaigns and they weren’t trying to necessarily communicate to a national audience.

A great example is James Talarico’s campaign. I got to know his speechwriter a little bit, and his campaign did something interesting there, which is they combined the speech writing and social media functions. They decided, “All right, this is a state rep in Texas who no one knows, and the way to become known is through storytelling. The oldest tactic in history.”.

According to recent reports, [Laughs] Are you really doing the end of Game of Thrones in my show right now, Jon? Come on. Don’t do this to me. No one liked it.

Right, no, me neither, me neither. Their social media presence was mostly TikTok, mostly Instagram, and it was just James Talarico telling stories really. It was giving speeches, but it was some of the oldest stories in human history, like David and Goliath. But I do think that [concerning] the whole “politicians as content creators” thing, there’s a way to do it where you are participating in the circus and then there’s a way to do it that is true to yourself and your values and the story you want to tell about where the country is and where you want to take it.

Sources indicate that if that story is compelling, then it will travel and break through even in this crowded media environment. The rise of vertical video allows for that kind of storytelling in a way that we haven’t seen in a while. After Barack Obama won the Iowa caucuses, we knew that every primary night he would get primetime coverage when he won and would be able to deliver a message to the whole country because everyone would be watching because it was primary night.

We really focused on those speeches. For Talarico’s campaign, and for a lot of these other Democrats now, they have a million of those moments every day, but they still have to do the storytelling in order for it to break through. The most successful candidates figured out how to do that storytelling in a really compelling way that wasn’t just “I’m going to tell a joke on Twitter” or “I’m going to do the hype reel” if I’m the House Oversight Committee.

Sources indicate that that is an effective way of getting people’s attention, but not necessarily holding their attention. If you are a politician today, you’ve got to figure out a way to get people’s attention, but then to hold it. And to hold it, you have to have a compelling story to tell.

My favorite piece of election day media was Rob Sand, the governor-elect of Iowa doing the Fleetwood Mac video where he drank the cranberry juice and longboard. I thought, this is great. I don’t know what the purpose of this video is, but I’m having a good time. And maybe that’s all you needed on this day was to just channel some vibes.

It has been revealed that then you got to actually go make some policy proposals. You have to fill potholes in Upcoming York City and then sit there and make videos about the filled potholes, which the Mamdani administration is particularly good at doing. Do you think this class of Democrats has that ability, even though they have a president who’s threatening to veto everything that they’re going to do?

I do think they have the ability. They’re going to be able to communicate. They’re going to be able to have hearings when they’re holding substantial tech CEOs and administration officials accountable. Those will be moments. They’re going to also have moments where they get to exert power over the government funding process.

Recent findings suggest that I personally think we’ll be headed towards several shutdowns because that’s going to be the main mechanism for Democrats to get their way. But also for the next two years, Donald Trump and the Congress are just not going to be the main focus. The main storyline of the next two years is going to be the presidential primaries.

I remember Democrats had a huge win in 2006, and then people can barely remember until the financial crisis what George Bush and the Democratic Congress were up to between 2006 and 2008, because everyone was focused on the Republican primary for president and the Democratic primary for president, because they were two wide open primaries. Once we get into 2027, you’re going to have a million primary debates on both sides.

Donald Trump’s obviously going to try to insert himself into the debate by trying to play kingmaker on the Republican side so that he can continue to get attention. And God forbid there are external events and crises that we have to deal with, then everyone’s going to be paying attention to Trump and the Congress. But the machinations of what’s happening inside the Congress I think will be the secondary story of the next two years.

In a recent development, you mentioned tech regulation. Actually, that’s where I want to end. I’ve often described hearings in Congress with tech CEOs as content capture sessions. That’s what we’re doing. Instead of Apple having the upcoming iPhone and all the creators rushing in to take photos of it, here’s Mark Zuckerberg and all the senators are going to rush to yell at him and we all make our videos and that’s the end of that. Nothing ever seems to happen.

Our audience is particularly nihilistic about it. You can yell at these CEOs all you want, but they just get their own way. There’s a lot of opportunity for oversight, particularly around AI, particularly Jensen Huang, the opportunity to do oversight over Nvidia and the Commerce Department and the FBI, whatever is happening. Boy, is there a lot of opportunity to oversight there.

In a recent development, how do you think that looks? We cover this often from a technology lens on the show. You cover it from a political lens on Offline. What do you think this looks like?

I know what I want it to look like. Because of where we are with AI development, I am more interested in oversight that actually changes the situation, that finally puts some guardrails or restrictions on the development of super intelligence, AGI, recursive self-improvement, whatever you want to call it, than just show trials where we all get to dunk on Mark Zuckerberg.

My biggest concern is we don’t have time to wait for a Democratic president or even a Republican president who’s actually going to do something to regulate the development of AI because by the time we get to 2028, it feels like the horse will have well left the barn. It’s already left the barn. I’m curious, over the next two years, can Democrats and Republicans in Congress actually force some kind of regulation or at least coordination among the AI giants to stop us from going off the cliff here?

Industry observers note that if I had to point to a realignment, it’s what I mentioned at the top. Surveillance feels like a glimmer of a realignment, and then data centers and AI feel like the glimmers of a realignment. You shouldn’t just take the economy away from people. Regardless of partisan lean, I think for most people, to your point about agency, feel you can’t just do that. You have to show up and make the case.

That is enough for a wholesale realignment. Those two issues are enough for these parties to totally scramble. And you’re going to get pro-business Democrats saying, “We’re going to have to do something to work with these guys.” You’re already seeing it. There’s James Talarico saying, “I wish Elon would just stay in his lane and stay out of politics, but we need him as a great businessman.”.

You’re seeing it on the Republican side: “We got this wrong. We need to regulate the Massive Tech companies. I’m anti-data center too.” In this environment where they basically have a little less than a year to make headway before the primary cycles begin, what do you think the steps are?

I worry that when I listen to a lot of these Democratic politicians and Republican politicians, all of them, there’s only a handful that seem to really understand the technology. You talk about regulation with people and they say, “Yeah, we need safeguards.” Safeguards could be anything from its effect on children and chatbots to making sure that we don’t lose human control of artificial intelligence.

Sources indicate that I feel like the cybersecurity stuff and the bio stuff — and then where recursive self-improvement goes — are the massive areas where I would want to see Democrats and Republicans get together. Even if they can’t pass laws because Trump doesn’t want to do anything to hurt the AI companies because he looks at it and notes, “The stock market’s tied to this, the economy’s tied to this, and I don’t want to do anything to hurt the economy and got to beat China and all that bullshit” — which is not bullshit — but you can’t answer every single concern about runaway artificial intelligence and losing control with the word “China.” Trump seems to be doing that and some other politicians as well.

History Notes a Bear Market Is Coming. Here's Exactly How I'm Preparing.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • 10 stocks we like better than Vanguard S&P 500 ETF ›.
  • A bear market occurs when a major index, such as the S&P 500, declines by at least 20% from its recent highs.
  • Sources indicate that nobody can definitively say when the next bear market will be; it could be next week, next month, next year, or next decade.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Stefon Walters – Nov 19, 2026 at 6:48AM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Vanguard S&P 500 ETF ›.

A bear market occurs when a major index, such as the S&P 500, declines by at least 20% from its recent highs. Of course, nobody likes seeing their portfolio lose value, but one truth can make investing less stressful once you digest it: Bear markets are unavoidable. They have always been part of the stock market cycle, and they always will be.

Sources indicate that nobody can definitively say when the next bear market will be; it could be next week, next month, next year, or next decade. A decade is probably far-fetched, but I wouldn't be surprised if we see one within the next year or so.

It has been revealed that either way, it's always better to be overprepared than underprepared. Here's one tangible move I personally make to prepare.

In a recent development, one strategy I lean on regardless of market conditions, but especially when there's more uncertainty than usual surrounding the market, is dollar-cost averaging into the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO +0.91%). When you dollar-cost average, you invest regularly at predetermined times, regardless of how the market is moving.

Recent findings suggest that I make bi-weekly investments in VOO, but the frequency should match your personal financial situation. It could be every Monday or on the same date every month. What matters most is sticking to your schedule because the whole point is investing without emotion. Once your schedule is set, it removes most of the emotion from investing.

Recent findings suggest that staying consistent with investing is much easier when prices are up because you don't want to miss out on gains. It's much harder when you expect prices to drop because you feel you can buy shares cheaper if you wait. The problem is that trying to time the market rarely works out consistently in investors' favor.

NYSEMKT · As of 9:39 AM ET 11/19/26.

I feel comfortable making regular investments in VOO, even during a bear market, because the S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.81%) has been one of the most dependable and resilient investments in all of the stock market for decades. VOO was created in September 2010, but the 500-stock S&P 500 we have today has been around since 1957.

It has been revealed that in the modern-day S&P 500's 69-year existence, it has experienced 11 bear markets. The length and severity have varied, but one thing has remained consistent: it has recovered and produced impressive long-term returns after each one:.

Industry observers note that data source: YCharts. Gains since trough based on S&P 500 level on Nov. 13.

You never want to use past events to assume something will always happen, but I fully expect this trend to continue as long as the stock market operates as we know it today.

With VOO (or any S&P 500 ETF), you're getting instant exposure to 500 of the largest U.S. companies on the market. And with an expense ratio of 0.03% ($0.30 per $1,000 invested), it's a cheap way to do so.

VOO holds companies across every major sector, with many longtime leaders that have stood the test of time and weathered plenty of storms. As long as the U.S. economy thrives over the long term, so will VOO -- even with the inevitable hiccups along the way.

Famed investor Warren Buffett echoed the same sentiment in a 2017 CNBC interview, saying investing in an S&P 500 ETF "makes the most sense practically all of the time" and that investors should "keep buying it through thick and thin, and especially through thin.".

Recent findings suggest that the last part is notable during a bear market. While many investors shy away from investing or sell, use bear markets as a chance to go "discount shopping." If you like a pair of shoes for $100, you'll likely love them even more at a 20%+ discount.

Recent findings suggest that again, we can't predict when the next bear market will happen, but it's undoubtedly a matter of when, not if. You can't control how things will play out, but you can make sure you remain consistent. Your future self will almost certainly thank you.

    TJX Beat Its Own Sales Forecast With 4% Comparable Growth, but Management Is Bracing for a Slower Holiday Quarter.

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (753 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • By Eric Volkman – Updated Nov 19, 2026 at 6:56AM EST.
    • One of the more stock-boosting quarterly reports from retailers this earnings season was published by TJX Companies (TJX -1.16%) on Wednesday.
    • Industry observers note that can it sustain that rise?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Eric Volkman – Updated Nov 19, 2026 at 6:56AM EST.

    One of the more stock-boosting quarterly reports from retailers this earnings season was published by TJX Companies (TJX -1.16%) on Wednesday. In the third quarter of fiscal 2027, the firm, known mainly for its TJ Maxx and Marshalls discount retail chains, posted comparable sales growth higher than it had forecast. Along with improved guidance and other encouraging developments, this excited investors about its future, driving the company's shares up more than 8% that day.

    Industry observers note that can it sustain that rise? It's forecasting comparable sales growth for the all-important holiday season lower than the actual third-quarter result, after all. Here's a brief look at whether that makes the stock a buy regardless.

    Those "comps" were 4% across all TJX's brands and geographies, which was reflected in a nearly 6% year-over-year increase in net sales, to $15.95 billion. GAAP net income climbed 7% to $1.54 billion, for earnings per share (EPS) of $1.39. However, $0.05 of that per-share figure was attributable to tariff refunds from the federal government (the duties it levied in 2025 were nixed in a Supreme Court decision this past February, hence the rebates). When adjusted for this, EPS was $1.34.

    That was in line with the consensus analyst estimate. TJX beat the average pundit projection of $15.82 billion for net sales, but not by much.

    In a recent development, there were heartening developments elsewhere in the earnings release. One was the broad improvement in comps, breaking down into 8% growth in the company's international reporting unit, 6% for TJX Canada, and 5% for the HomeGoods brand. On a more downbeat note, the flagship Marmaxx unit (the company's TJ Maxx and Marshalls operations in the U.S.) only inched 2% higher.

    In a recent development, the company now expects full-year comps to rise by 4%; previously it proffered a range of 3% to 4%. It also raised the lower end of its adjusted EPS estimate range to $5.17 per share from $5.15. It kept the ceiling intact, at $5.20.

    Industry observers note that although TJX's guidance for the current holiday quarter is below its full-year outlook, at 2% to 3%, management asserts that it's well-primed for the shopping season. In the conference call discussing its third-quarter performance, CEO Ernie Herrman provided some color about the two distinct marketing pushes that will support its leading brands -- Never Uniform, Always You for TJ Maxx, and Holiday Hustlers for Marshalls.

    "We are targeting both new and existing shoppers across a wide consumer demographic of varying ages and income levels, and leaning into digital channels that align with today's consumer media habits," Herrman remarked. "We feel great about our social media strategies and believe they will drive high engagement.".

    Judging by the 30-second spots for both campaigns I viewed, they do a decent job flagging the strengths of each brand. TJ Maxx, with its proportionally larger selection for female shoppers, sharply targets women with Never Uniform, Always You. Holiday Hustlers emphasizes the deals on quality merchandise that Marshalls is theoretically capable of engineering.

    In a recent development, the Wednesday pop feels like something of a relief rally to me, as TJX's shares have slumped this year in the wake of less inspiring quarters. There were numerous things to like about the company's third-quarter performance, sure, but I’d be concerned that the comparable-sales growth guidance for the holiday frame is notably below the full-year estimate. It's also well underneath the 5% TJX achieved in the same period in both fiscal 2025 and 2026.

    NYSE · As of 9:38 AM ET 11/19/26.

    Meanwhile, on valuations, the organization's stock is pricier than non-discount retailers that, in my view, have performed better lately. Its 22-plus forward P/E feels high compared to the levels for those peers, which are currently hovering in the low- to mid-teens in the run-up to shopping season.

    While I don't think TJX is doing badly, to me it's not enough of an outperformer for its stock to be compelling. I also think there are better bargains elsewhere in the broader retail sector right now.

    I Didn’t Know Southwest Points Could Be This Valuable

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1642 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nerdwallet

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that in a world of transferable points currencies, you might not think holding an airline or hotel credit card is necessary.
    • Take Southwest Airlines, for example.
    • In a recent development, "Experiences create lifetime memories,” notes Nandika Suri, Southwest’s vice president of Rapid Rewards.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that in a world of transferable points currencies, you might not think holding an airline or hotel credit card is necessary. But travel brands are pushing back against that narrative, offering exclusive perks and redemption packages to those who carry their cards.

    Take Southwest Airlines, for example. Its Rapid Rewards loyalty program allows you to redeem points for flights, but it also offers a special program called Rapid Rewards Access Events exclusively for Southwest credit cardholders. In exchange for a decent chunk of points, you can get a vacation package that’s worth significantly more than the price you pay. Instead of a traditional flight award redemption, you get a cohesive travel experience.

    In a recent development, "Experiences create lifetime memories,” notes Nandika Suri, Southwest’s vice president of Rapid Rewards. “For us, we really want them to have great memories and remember our brand as part of that.”.

    It has been revealed that southwest invited me to participate in one of its Rapid Rewards Access Events. While Southwest covered the cost of my trip, these opinions are my own. Here’s what I learned.

    Every event is different (ranging from concerts to multiday trips), but big-ticket Rapid Rewards Access Events tend to include flights, hotel accommodations, meals and excursions.

    Recent findings suggest that the event I participated in was in Maui to celebrate the 30th anniversary of Southwest and Chase’s partnership. This was a bigger production than the typical event, with about 60 cardholders (and a plus one) participating. A typical multiday event might have 20 or 25 packages for sale.

    In exchange for 275,000 Rapid Rewards points, cardholders received for themselves and one guest:.

    A four-night stay in an ocean-view room at the Grand Wailea, a Waldorf Astoria Resort, in Maui, including daily breakfast.

    Ground transportation between the airport and the resort, as well as for any scheduled group activities.

    A special welcome reception and farewell dinner.

    A snorkeling cruise with lunch and beverages included.

    A choice between several excursions, including a spa treatment, golf, ziplining and more.

    According to recent reports, even at extremely conservative estimates, I would value all of those things at roughly $4,600. That’s $750 more than what NerdWallet values 275,000 Rapid Rewards points at, according to our 2026 data. If we took a more liberal approach, I think it would be fair to say the package was worth more than $7,000. That puts this redemption between 1.7 and 2.5 cents per point. (Expand the section below to see how I arrived at those numbers.).

    As of 2026, NerdWallet values Southwest Rapid Rewards points at 1.4 cents apiece. That puts the 275,000-point Southwest event package at $3,850.

    Let’s put some numbers to the package inclusions and see how the points price stacks up to the cash valuation.

    $1,000 Southwest gift card: It’s pretty easy to value a $1,000 Southwest gift card at $1,000. You need to fly to the event, so that can be taken at face value. (You could also use it toward a different trip, if you wanted to use points or fly with a different carrier.).

    It has been revealed that four-night hotel stay: For the Grand Wailea stay, a nonrefundable Hilton Honors discount rate for an ocean-view room on the exact same dates in 2027 costs $4,490.19, after factoring in taxes and fees. (The base-level terrace-view room would cost $3,992.17.).

    If you were to use points, a standard room without an ocean view would cost 130,000 Hilton points per night. An ocean-view room’s rate shoots up to 281,000 Hilton points per night.

    Using NerdWallet’s 2026 valuation of Hilton points at 0.4 cent per point, that puts the value of the two rooms at $2,080 and $4,496, respectively. To make things interesting, let’s say the hotel stay is worth $2,080.

    Sources indicate that daily breakfast at the hotel buffet is about $60 per person, before tax and tip. For four days, let’s put that at around another $500, bringing the total stay value to $2,580.

    Industry observers note that ground transportation: Let’s make things simple and just say it’s $30 each way between the airport and the resort. For two people, that would be worth $120.

    Welcome reception and farewell dinner: Southwest and Chase put a lot of effort into making these events nice, from the food and free-flowing alcohol to the entertainment (there was even a fire performance at the farewell dinner).

    I would value this at $50 per person, conservatively, or $200 total.

    Snorkeling cruise: I went on Viator to find a similar experience, and the cheapest option I found was priced at $100 per person.

    Again, let’s price it conservatively and say it’s worth $200. That price doesn't include hotel transportation, gratuities, towels or alcoholic beverages, while the Southwest package did.

    Excursion choice: Southwest let everyone choose an excursion, ranging from a chill pool or spa day to ziplining through the jungle or learning to surf.

    It’s hard to put a number on this, because the activities varied in cost.

    According to recent reports, I went ziplining, and it was $240 for six lines. That price doesn’t include transportation to the excursion, which was covered by Southwest. Meanwhile, a standard massage at the hotel spa is $275 (and that doesn’t even factor in the 20% service charge).

    Let’s put this at $250 per person, giving us a round $500 for two people’s excursions.

    Grand total: Summing up these numbers gets us $4,600. That’s $750 more than the $3,850 NerdWallet values 275,000 points at, but keep in mind that we probably undervalued several of the inclusions. The actual value of a trip like this could be much higher.

    It also doesn’t factor in other things, like snacks provided at the hospitality booth, as well as surprise gifts and goodie bags prepared by Southwest and Chase for attendees.

    Before you book a Rapid Rewards Access Event, there are some drawbacks to booking a vacation this way.

    The biggest one is if you don’t like group trips or following a schedule on your vacations. Given the nature of these events, you’ll be surrounded by a group of travelers, many of whom will likely be longtime Southwest flyers. If you prefer to keep to yourself, then this type of trip is likely not a good fit.

    You’ll also have multiple scheduled activities on your itinerary. While you can choose to not show up, those activities add a lot of value to the trip.

    With that mentioned, I found the itinerary quite laid back. The amount of scheduled activities wasn’t overwhelming, and there was plenty of free time to do whatever you wanted. One couple I met even rented a car and explored Maui in their downtime, so they kept themselves busy.

    These events are extremely popular, and many attendees I met at the Maui event had been on multiple Southwest cardmember trips.

    It has been revealed that scoring a ticket to a Rapid Rewards Access Event might even require setting your alarm for when tickets drop. Several cardmembers told me they’ve experienced times when the event they wanted was sold out in hours, if not minutes. (The Maui one took a few hours to sell out, because it was larger than most.).

    It has been revealed that finally, 275,000 points is a lot — even if you're getting great value. If your Rapid Rewards points are collecting dust in your account, then it could make sense. But if you have a transferable currency, then you'd have to weigh whether you might get better value elsewhere, such as booking round-trip business class flights.

    Southwest isn’t the only airline or travel brand to offer special events for cardholders. United Airlines has MileagePlus Exclusives and United Card Events from Chase; Delta Air Lines offers cardmember-exclusive redemptions in its SkyMiles Experiences program; and Marriott has its Marriott Bonvoy Moments program.

    But every redemption option is different — even if it’s within the same loyalty program. For example, some Rapid Rewards Access Events are packages you can purchase immediately for a set price, while others are auction-style listings. Some programs offer paid experiences, so you can only pay in cash, not points.

    Personally, I’m a fan of the fixed-price points option. You know the upfront price, and you don’t have to worry about getting into a last-minute bidding war that could lead you to paying more than you intended. Plus, Southwest has historically had limited award redemption options, although that will change in 2027 when it allows international partner award bookings.

    Ultimately, whether you think a Rapid Rewards Access Event is a worthwhile redemption will depend on your interests, and Southwest is working to expand its offerings to meet people’s passions.

    "We do offer a lot of breadth because we want to get different types of customers engaged with different types of things based on their individual passion points and what they're really interested in,” says Suri, the Rapid Rewards chief.

    If you’d rather spend time in the mountains than on the beach, you might not want to spend 275,000 Rapid Rewards points on the Maui package.

    Instead, you probably would've been interested in the 250,000-point package for "Boots, Bourbon and Bonfires" — a three-day trip to Devil's Thumb Ranch, an upscale dude ranch resort about 1.5 hours outside of Denver.

    Before you book, just remember: You’ll need a Southwest credit card to purchase.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Chris Neiger – Nov 19, 2026 at 7:02AM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing ›.

    Sources indicate that the artificial intelligence trade feels unstable, to say the least, right now. Several months ago, investors began questioning how much tech companies were spending on AI infrastructure. And the recent resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang further heightened investor skepticism that all is well with AI companies.

    Even AI darlings, including Broadcom and Marvell Technology, have fallen as shareholders wonder if spending on new AI chips is sustainable.

    Industry observers note that but if we zoom out and look at the broader trajectory of AI, it's clear that over the current decade, tech companies will need more AI chips than they do now, not fewer. They'll also be used in more devices than before, including robotics.

    Industry observers note that so, which AI chip company is poised to benefit the most through 2030, as AI demand accelerates? I think there's a good chance it'll be Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM +2.58%), the leading manufacturer of AI chips. Here's why TSMC is perfectly positioned to win over the next few years.

    According to recent reports, one of the most important reasons to consider owning Taiwan Semiconductor (also referred to as TSMC) is that it's the world's leading processor manufacturer. TSMC holds about 73% of the chip foundry market, by revenue, far outpacing its closest rival, Samsung, which has just 6%. It's worth letting that sink in for just a moment because it means that nearly three-quarters of foundry revenue (chip production by a manufacturer) comes from just one company.

    That's an enormous competitive advantage for TSMC, and the far-and-away lead means that the competition will have a very hard time catching up. If that were TSMC's only competitive advantage, it would be enough to warrant owning the stock, but it also has another competitive angle.

    It holds an estimated 90% market share for the most advanced processors.

    In a recent development, it's not enough for TSMC to just manufacture chips; the company is also far ahead of competitors at making the most advanced processors for AI. This matters because manufacturing chips is expensive and difficult. To do it right, companies need the best equipment, lots of experience, and need to produce chips with high yield rates (usable chips).

    In short, no other company makes more revenue from making processors than TSMC, and no one makes chips more efficiently than TSMC.

    That's why Nvidia and Apple are TSMC's two biggest customers: they need lots of high-end processors made as efficiently as possible. Not to mention, it also makes chips for Broadcom, AMD, Intel, Qualcomm, and many other AI companies.

    NYSE · As of 9:40 AM ET 11/19/26.

    Industry observers note that there are plenty of AI companies that can't back up their rapid share price growth with sales and earnings -- but Taiwan Semiconductor isn't one of them. The company is already experiencing impressive top- and bottom-line growth, with revenue rising about 41% in the third quarter (which ended Sept. 30) to $46.72 billion and the company notched its sixth straight quarter of record profit -- up 69% from the year-ago quarter.

    According to recent reports, and there appears to be plenty more where that came from. Management issued fourth-quarter revenue guidance between $52.3 billion and $54.3 billion, representing an increase of 58% from the year-ago quarter. And TSMC's leadership indicates that its AI accelerator (specialized GPUs and server AI processors) revenue will grow at a compounded annual rate in the high-50% range through 2029.

    It has been revealed that TSMC is benefiting from a surge in AI spending that, despite some investor fears, isn't slowing down. A recent Bank of America report claims technology companies will likely double their spending on AI infrastructure over the next two years, reaching more than $2 trillion.

    And even as TSMC is geared up to benefit from more AI chip demand, you don't have to pay a premium for its shares. Taiwan Semiconductor's stock has a trailing price-to-earnings ratio of 25.8, which is on par with the tech sector P/E average of about 26.

    All of which means that Taiwan Semiconductor's potential between now and 2030 remains very high as the company successfully taps into the expanding AI chip market and maintains its lead in global chip manufacturing.

    Given that TSMC stock has traded down almost 17% over the past three months amid a broader market sell-off, now might be a good time to buy on the dip.

    #39113. What to Buy (and Skip) on Black Friday 2026
